p.src: Now Li Kui had knocked the young woman down with a jab of his finger. The tavern keeper barred his way and cried, “Gentlemen, what are we to do?” In a panic, the keeper called the servers and attendants to help her. They laid her on the floor and sprayed water over her until she gradually revived, then helped her up. On examination, a patch of skin had been scraped from her temple, causing her to faint. Once she had been revived, all was well. When her parents heard that he was the Black Whirlwind, they were so terrified that they stood dazed for a long while, not daring to utter a word. The young woman was already able to speak. Her mother took a handkerchief and bound her head herself, then gathered up her hairpins and ornaments. Song Jiang asked, “What is your surname? Where are you from?” The old woman replied, “To tell you the truth, sir, my husband and I are surnamed Song and originally came from the capital. We have only this daughter, whose childhood name is Yulian. Her father taught her a few songs, and we somehow make a living by having her sing here at the Pipa Pavilion. She is hasty by nature and failed to read the situation. Ignoring what you gentlemen were saying, she simply began to sing. Today this good man struck her accidentally and hurt her a little, but we could hardly file a complaint with the authorities and cause you trouble.” Seeing that she spoke honestly and humbly, Song Jiang said, “Have someone come with me to the prison camp. I shall give you twenty taels of silver to nurse your daughter back to health and later marry her to a good man, so she need no longer sing here for money.” The couple bowed in gratitude and said, “How could we dare hope for so much?” Song Jiang said, “When I give my word, I keep it. I never lie. Have your old man come with me at once to collect it for her.” The husband and wife bowed their thanks, saying, “We are deeply grateful for your aid, sir.” Dai Zong reproached Li Kui: “Whenever you start a quarrel, you rogue, you make our brother waste another great sum of silver.” Li Kui replied, “My finger only brushed her lightly, and she fell over by herself. I have never seen such a damned woman so delicate. You could punch me in the face a hundred times and it would do me no harm.” Song Jiang and all the others burst out laughing. Zhang Shun promptly told a server, “Tell them I shall pay for this banquet myself.” Hearing this, the server said, “It is no trouble, no trouble. Please go on your way.” Song Jiang would not hear of it. “Brother, I invited you two here to drink. How could I let you pay?” Zhang Shun insisted on paying, saying, “It is a rare blessing to meet you, elder brother. When you were in Shandong, my brother and I had already wished to come and join you. By Heaven’s favor I have beheld your honored face today, so let this merely express my humble regard; it is far too little to count as a proper gift.” Dai Zong said, “Brother Gongming, since this is Second Brother Zhang’s sincere token of respect, you should graciously consent.” Song Jiang said, “Since you have paid, brother, I shall arrange another cup of wine another day to return your courtesy.” Zhang Shun was delighted. Taking the two carp, he and Dai Zong and Li Kui escorted old Song with Song Jiang away from the Pipa Pavilion and back to the prison camp. All five entered the clerks’ office and sat down. Song Jiang first took out two small ingots totaling twenty taels and gave them to old Song. The old man bowed his thanks and departed; there is no more to tell of it. It was already late. Zhang Shun delivered the fish, and Song Jiang took out Zhang Heng’s letter and handed it to him. Then they bade farewell and Zhang Shun left. Song Jiang then took out a large silver ingot of fifty taels and said to Li Kui, “Brother, take this for your expenses.” Dai Zong and Li Kui also took their leave and hurried back into the city.

p.src: Now Song Jiang gave one of the fish to the prison governor and kept the other to eat himself. Finding the fish fresh and delicious, Song Jiang indulged his appetite and ate too much. By the fourth watch that night, his bowels were twisting and churning with pain; by dawn he had suffered diarrhea some twenty times, then fainted and lay unconscious in his room. Song Jiang treated people with the greatest kindness, so everyone in the camp came to cook porridge, heat broth, attend him, and nurse him. The next day, knowing how fond Song Jiang was of fish, Zhang Shun brought him two more fine, golden carp and came to thank him for forwarding the letter. Instead he found Song Jiang prostrated in bed with violent diarrhea, while all the prisoners watched over him in the room. At the sight, Zhang Shun wished to summon a physician, but Song Jiang said, “I merely indulged my appetite, ate too much fresh fish, and upset my stomach. Just buy me one dose of Liuhe decoction to stop the diarrhea, and I shall be well.” He told Zhang Shun to give one of the two fish to Governor Wang and the other to Warden Zhao. After delivering the fish, Zhang Shun bought a dose of Liuhe decoction and brought it to Song Jiang, then returned home. There is no more to tell of this. The men in the camp decocted the medicine and tended him. The next day, Dai Zong and Li Kui prepared wine and meat and went straight to the clerks’ office to visit Song Jiang. They found that Song Jiang had only just begun to recover from his sudden illness and could eat neither wine nor meat. So the two consumed it themselves before his room, remaining until evening, when they bade him farewell and left. There is no more to tell of this.

p.src: Song Jiang rested and recuperated in the camp for five or seven days. Feeling sound again and fully recovered, he thought of going into the city to find Dai Zong. Another day passed, yet not one of them came to see him. The following day, after breakfast, around the hour of the dragon, he tucked some silver into his clothes, locked his door, and left the camp. He strolled into the street, made his way into the city, and near the left side of the prefectural offices asked where Superintendent Dai lived. Someone told him, “He has neither wife nor children and lodges in the Guanyin Hermitage beside the City God Temple.” Hearing this, Song Jiang sought out the place, but by the time he arrived, the door was locked and Dai Zong had gone out. He then asked after Li Kui, the Black Whirlwind, and many people replied, “He is a wandering devil without ties or family and merely makes his quarters in the prison. Like an inspector with no fixed post, he sleeps two days in the east and lounges several in the west. No one truly knows where he lives.” When Song Jiang next asked after Zhang Shun, the fish broker, someone else said, “He lives in a village outside the city; even when selling fish, he stays by the river outside the walls. He comes into the city only to collect money owed to him.”

p.src: After hearing this, Song Jiang went back out of the city, determined to ask his way all the way to Zhang Shun’s home. Alone and deeply dejected, he wandered beyond the city once more. There he saw a magnificent sweep of river scenery upon which he could never gaze his fill. As he passed before a tavern, he looked up and saw beside it a tall signpole bearing a blue-cloth wine banner inscribed: “Official Xunyang River Wine Depot.” Outside the carved eaves hung a signboard bearing the three characters “Xunyang Tower,” boldly brushed by Su Dongpo. Seeing it, Song Jiang said, “When I was in Yuncheng County, I heard only that Jiangzhou possessed the splendid Xunyang Tower. So this is where it stands. Though I am here alone, I must not miss the chance. Why not go upstairs and look around for a while?” When Song Jiang reached the front of the tower, he saw vermilion ornamental posts beside the entrance and two whitewashed boards upon the pillars, each bearing five large characters: “Wine unmatched beneath the heavens; a tower renowned throughout the world.” Song Jiang went upstairs and took a seat in a private chamber overlooking the river; leaning on the railing and raising his eyes, he saw that it was indeed a magnificent tavern. p.src: Carved eaves gleamed in the sunlight, and painted beams seemed to soar into the clouds. Jade-green balustrades ran low beneath the windows, while emerald curtains hung high over the casements. A drunken gaze might lose itself against the blue heavens and ten thousand folds of cloud-wreathed hills; a poet's soul might be stirred by the river's misty waters, billowing like auspicious snow. At the white duckweed ferry, the clatter of fishermen's oars could be heard from time to time; by the red smartweed shoals, old anglers were often seen beating time with their paddles. Wild birds sang in the green scholar trees beside the tower, while flower-decked steeds stamped beneath the emerald willows before the gate.

p.src: When Song Jiang had finished looking, he could not stop exclaiming in admiration. A waiter came upstairs and asked, “Sir, are you expecting guests, or merely amusing yourself?” Song Jiang replied, “I am expecting two guests, but they have not yet arrived. Bring me first a jar of good wine, and serve whatever fruits and meats you have—but no fish.” The waiter heard him and went downstairs. Before long he returned upstairs with a tray. He set down a jar of fine Blue Bridge Moon-and-Breeze wine, vegetables, fresh seasonal fruits, and dishes to accompany the wine—several kinds of fat mutton, tender chicken, stuffed goose, and choice pork—all served on vermilion plates and saucers. Song Jiang looked upon it all and secretly rejoiced, saying admiringly to himself, “Such well-ordered delicacies and such elegant vessels—Jiangzhou is truly a splendid place. Though I was banished here for a crime, I have at least seen some true mountains and true waters. My homeland may have several famed mountains and ancient sites, but it possesses no scenery like this.” All alone, he drank cup after cup at the railing until, before he knew it, he was deeply intoxicated. Suddenly a thought surged into his mind: “I was born in Shandong and raised in Yuncheng. Trained as a clerk, I made the acquaintance of so many gallant men of the rivers and lakes. Yet though I gained an empty reputation, I am now past thirty without fame or fortune, and instead have had both cheeks branded and been sent into exile here; how shall I ever see my aged father and my brother in my homeland again?” As the wine rose within him, tears streamed unbidden down his face. The wind and all he saw stirred his emotions, and resentment and sorrow filled his heart. All at once he composed a lyric to the tune “Moon over the West River” and called for the waiter, asking to borrow brush and inkstone. Rising to look around, he saw many verses left by earlier visitors upon a whitewashed wall. Song Jiang thought, “Why should I not write mine here? p.src: After finishing the poem, Song Jiang wrote five large characters beneath it: “Composed by Song Jiang of Yuncheng.” When he had finished, he tossed the brush onto the table and sang to himself for a while. After several more cups he became insensibly dead drunk, unable to withstand the wine. He called the waiter to reckon the bill, took out some silver, and gave the entire surplus to the waiter as a tip before flicking his sleeves and descending the stairs. Staggering and stumbling, he made his way back to the prison camp. He opened his room, fell straight onto the bed, and slept without waking until the fifth watch. When he sobered, he had utterly forgotten the whole affair of inscribing the poem at the Xunyang River Tower the previous day. Suffering from the effects of the wine, he simply lay sleeping in his room; no more need be said of that.

p.src: Now across the river from Jiangzhou stood another town called Wuwei Military Prefecture, a remote and rustic place. In the town lived an assistant prefect then out of office, surnamed Huang and given the name Wenbing. Though this man had read the Classics, he was a sycophantic flatterer, narrow and mean of heart, forever envying the worthy and resenting the capable. He harmed those superior to himself and tormented those beneath him, devoting himself to victimizing the people of his district. Learning that Prefect Cai the Ninth was the son of Grand Tutor Cai at the imperial court, he repeatedly ingratiated himself with him and often crossed the river to pay his respects, hoping Cai would recommend him for an appointment so that he might hold office again. It was Song Jiang's fate to suffer, and so he crossed paths with this enemy. That day Huang Wenbing was sitting idly at home with nothing to divert him. Taking two servants and some newly purchased seasonal gifts, he crossed the river in his own swift boat and went directly to the prefectural offices to visit Prefect Cai the Ninth. Unfortunately, he found a public banquet in progress at the offices and dared not enter. He therefore returned to his boat, which his servants happened to have moored beneath the Xunyang Tower. Finding the weather warm, Huang Wenbing decided to go upstairs and amuse himself for a while. He strolled into the tavern, looked around, then went up to the drinking hall and leaned upon the railing for diversion. He saw that many verses had been inscribed on the walls; some were well composed, while others were sheer nonsense. Huang Wenbing read them and sneered. When he came to Song Jiang's lyric “Moon over the West River” and the four lines of verse accompanying it, he exclaimed in astonishment, “Is this not a seditious poem? Who wrote it here?” Beneath it were written five large characters: “Composed by Song Jiang of Yuncheng.” Huang Wenbing read again: “From childhood I studied Classics and histories; grown to manhood, I too possess stratagems.” He sneered, “This fellow thinks no little of himself.” He continued: “Like a fierce tiger lying on a barren hill, I hide my claws and fangs and endure.” Huang Wenbing said, “The scoundrel is clearly one who will not keep to his proper place.” Again he read: “Ill fortune branded both my cheeks; how can I bear exile in Jiangzhou?” Huang Wenbing said, “He is no man of lofty ideals. Evidently he is merely a convict in exile.” Again he read: “If in years to come I can avenge my wrongs, blood shall stain the mouth of the Xunyang River.” Huang Wenbing said, “On whom does this scoundrel mean to take revenge? He means to stir up trouble here! You are nothing but an exiled convict—what could you possibly accomplish?” Then he read the poem: “My heart is in Shandong though my body dwells in Wu; like drifting tumbleweed over rivers and seas, I sigh in vain.” Huang Wenbing said, “These two lines might still be forgiven.” He read on: “If someday I fulfill my soaring ambition, I shall dare laugh that Huang Chao was no true man!” Huang Wenbing shook his head. “What insolence! He means to surpass Huang Chao. What can that be but an intention to rebel?” Looking once more at the words “Composed by Song Jiang of Yuncheng,” Huang Wenbing said, “I have often heard this name. The man is most likely some petty clerk.” He summoned the waiter and asked, “Who exactly was the man who inscribed these two pieces of verse here?” The waiter replied, “Last night a man drank a whole jar of wine by himself. Once drunk, he became wild and unrestrained and wrote them here.” Huang Wenbing asked, “What sort of man was he, roughly?” The waiter replied, “He had two lines of official brands on his cheeks, so he was most likely a man from the prison camp. He was dark, short, and stout.” Huang Wenbing said, “That is he.” He promptly borrowed brush and inkstone, obtained a sheet of paper, and copied the writings down. Tucking the copy into his clothes, he instructed the waiter not to scrape the originals away.

p.src: When Dai Zong heard this, he was startled and inwardly cried out in dismay. He immediately left the prefectural offices and mustered the warders and jailers, ordering each man to go home, fetch his weapons, and assemble at the City God Temple beside Dai Zong’s lodgings. After giving them these instructions and sending them home, Dai Zong invoked his magic traveling art and hastened ahead to the penal camp, going straight into the clerks’ office. He pushed open the door and found Song Jiang inside. Seeing Dai Zong enter, Song Jiang hurried forward to greet him and said, “When I came into town the other day, there was nowhere I did not search for you. But you were away, and being alone with nothing to do, I went up Xunyang Tower and drank a flask of wine. For the past two days I have felt dazed and unwell, and have been lying here with a hangover.” Dai Zong asked, “Brother, what words did you write upon the tower the other day?” Song Jiang replied, “Wild words spoken in drunkenness—who could remember them?” Dai Zong said, “Just now the prefect summoned me before the court and issued an order that I take many men with me and ‘seize Song Jiang of Yuncheng County, the criminal who inscribed a seditious poem at Xunyang Tower, and bring the man himself before the authorities.’ I was badly startled, so first I contrived to keep the constables waiting at the City God Temple. Now I have come ahead especially to warn you, Brother. What are we to do? How can we save you?” Upon hearing this, Song Jiang scratched his head without knowing where it itched and could only cry in despair, “This time I am surely going to die.” Dai Zong said, “I have one expedient that may free you, Brother, though I do not know what you will think of it. I dare not delay now. I must return and come with the others to arrest you. Loosen your hair, splash urine and filth over the floor, then lie down in it and pretend to be raving mad. When I arrive with the men, babble nonsense and act as though you have lost your wits. I shall go and report to the prefect on your behalf.” Song Jiang said, “Thank you, worthy brother, for your guidance. I beg you to do all you can to protect me.”

p.src: Dai Zong hurriedly took leave of Song Jiang and returned to the city. He went straight to the Temple of the City God, summoned the constables, and led them directly into the prison compound. Feigning severity, he demanded, “Which one is the newly exiled prisoner Song Jiang?” The ward chief led them to the clerks’ room, where they saw Song Jiang with his hair hanging loose, rolling in a cesspit of urine and excrement. My father-in-law commanded me to lead a hundred thousand heavenly troops here to slaughter you people of Jiangzhou. King Yama is my vanguard, the Generals of the Five Paths guard the rear, and I have been given a golden seal weighing more than eight hundred jin, with which I shall kill scum like you.” The constables said, “So he is a madman who has lost his wits. What use would there be in taking him away?” Dai Zong said, “You are right. Let us go back and report for now. If they still want him seized, we can return.” The men followed Dai Zong back to the prefectural offices, where Prefect Cai Jiu was waiting in the hall for their report. From below the hall, Dai Zong and the constables reported to the prefect, “It turns out that Song Jiang is a man who has lost his mind. He pays no heed to the filth of urine and excrement, babbles incoherently, and is covered in an unbearable stench of dung. We therefore dared not bring him here.”

p.src: Prefect Cai Jiu looked at him and did not know what to make of the matter. Huang Wenbing again said to the prefect, “Summon the prison compound’s superintendent, clerk, and ward chief, and ask them whether this man was mad when he arrived or became mad only recently. If he was mad when he arrived, then the illness is genuine. If he became mad only recently, he must be feigning it.” The prefect said, “Your words are entirely sound.” He sent men to summon the prison superintendent and clerk. When the two were questioned, they dared conceal nothing and had to answer truthfully, “This man showed no sign of madness when he arrived. We suppose the affliction has appeared only recently.” The prefect flew into a rage when he heard this. He called the jailers and guards forward. They bound Song Jiang, threw him down, and dealt him fifty strokes in succession, beating him until he seemed to die and return to life, his skin split and flesh torn, fresh blood streaming everywhere. Dai Zong watched in anguish, but could think of no way to save him. At first Song Jiang continued babbling nonsense, but eventually he could no longer endure the torture and confessed, “In a moment of drunkenness, I wrongly wrote a seditious poem. I had no other intent.” Prefect Cai Jiu immediately took down his confession, fastened a twenty-five-jin condemned prisoner’s cangue around his neck, and had him thrust into the main prison under confinement. Song Jiang’s legs had been beaten so badly that he could not walk. The cangue was nailed shut there in the hall, and he was escorted directly to death row. Only through Dai Zong’s unstinting efforts was he protected, for Dai Zong instructed all the junior jailers to take good care of him. Dai Zong himself arranged meals and provisions for Song Jiang, but of this there is no need to speak further.

p.src: That day Dai Zong left Jiangzhou and traveled until evening, when he sought rest at an inn. He removed the magic-horse talismans and burned several hundred sheets of spirit money as an offering. After spending the night, he rose early the next morning, ate and drank, left the inn, fastened on the four magic-horse talismans again, shouldered the dispatch hampers, and strode swiftly away. Truly, wind and rain roared past his ears, and his feet seemed never to touch the ground. Along the road he ate a little vegetarian food, drank some meatless wine, took a snack, and hurried onward. As dusk approached, Dai Zong stopped early and found another inn where he lodged for the night. The next day he rose in the fifth watch to take advantage of the cool morning, fastened on the magic-horse talismans, shouldered the dispatch hampers, and set off again. After traveling some two or three hundred li, it was already around the hour of the Snake, yet he had not seen a single decent tavern. It was early in the sixth month, and the steaming heat made sweat pour from him like rain until his whole body was drenched. He also feared he might suffer heatstroke. Just when hunger and thirst tormented him, he saw ahead, beside a grove, a tavern standing by the water at the edge of a lake. In the flick of a finger Dai Zong reached it. Looking inside, he found it spotlessly clean, with twenty sets of seats, all furnished with red-lacquered tables and stools, and a continuous row of latticed windows. Dai Zong carried the dispatch hampers inside, chose a secure seat, set the hampers down, removed the sash from his waist, and took off his apricot-yellow shirt. Spraying it with a mouthful of water, he spread it over the window rail to air. Once Dai Zong was seated, a waiter came over and asked, “How much wine shall I bring you, sir? What meat would you like with it—pork, mutton, or beef?” Dai Zong replied, “Not much wine. Just prepare me some rice to eat.” The waiter said, “We sell both wine and rice here, and we also have steamed buns and noodle soup.” Dai Zong said, “I do not eat meat or fish. What vegetarian broth do you have to go with rice?” The waiter replied, “How about richly seasoned spicy braised tofu?” Dai Zong said, “Excellent, excellent.” Before long the waiter returned with a bowl of braised tofu, set down two dishes of vegetables, and poured three large bowls of wine in succession. The servants had just hoisted Dai Zong up and were carrying him into the slaughter room to cut him open when a shoulder bag slipped down beside the bench, with a vermilion-and-green lacquered identification tablet hanging from it. Zhu Gui picked it up and saw silver characters carved upon it: “Dai Zong, chief prison warden of the two courts of Jiangzhou.” After reading it, Zhu Gui said, “Stay your hands. I have often heard our strategist speak of a man in Jiangzhou called Dai Zong, the ‘Magic Traveler,’ one of his dearest friends. Can this be the very man? Why, then, would he be carrying a letter meant to bring harm to Song Jiang? By great good fortune, this letter has fallen into my hands. Have the servants give him the antidote and revive him first; then I shall question him and learn the truth of the matter.” The servants immediately mixed the antidote with water, propped Dai Zong up, and poured it down his throat. In a moment Dai Zong’s brow relaxed, his eyes opened wide, and he scrambled to his feet. Seeing Zhu Gui holding the opened family letter and reading it, Dai Zong shouted, “Who are you? When Chao Gai heard this, he hurriedly invited Warden Dai to sit and questioned him closely about what had brought Third Brother Song into this lawsuit. Dai Zong recounted, one matter after another, how Song Jiang had composed the seditious poem. Chao Gai was greatly shocked. He immediately rose to summon the chieftains, muster their troops, descend the mountain, attack Jiangzhou, and rescue Third Brother Song to the stronghold. Wu Yong remonstrated, “Brother, you must not act rashly. Jiangzhou lies far from here. If our troops go there, I fear we shall only invite disaster, beat the grass and startle the snake, and instead cause Song Gongming’s death. This affair cannot be won by force; it can only be accomplished by stratagem. Though I possess little talent, I can devise a small stratagem centered upon Warden Dai that will surely save Third Brother Song’s life.” Chao Gai said, “We should like to hear your ingenious plan, Strategist.” Wu the Scholar said, “Prefect Cai Jiu has sent the Warden to the Eastern Capital with a letter seeking the Grand Preceptor’s reply. We shall turn that very letter to our advantage, forge a reply, and have the Warden carry it back. The letter will say only: ‘The criminal Song Jiang must under no circumstances be executed there. You are to select reliable officers and secretly escort him to the Eastern Capital, where he shall be questioned in detail, publicly executed after judgment, and thus the children’s rhyme put to rest.’ When they escort him past this region, we shall send men down the mountain and seize him. What do you think of this plan?” Chao Gai said, “But if they do not pass this way, will that not ruin the whole enterprise?” Gongsun Sheng said, “What difficulty is there in that? We shall send men to gather intelligence far and near. Wherever they pass, we shall make certain to be waiting and seize him at any cost. I fear only that they may fail to send him under escort.”

What business brings you here?” After bowing, Dai Zong said, “I am a temple attendant who prepares offerings at the Temple of the Sacred Peak in Taianzhou. We are now rebuilding the Tower of the Five Sacred Peaks, and the wealthy families of our prefecture wish to have an inscription carved on a stele. They have therefore sent me especially with fifty taels of silver for your household expenses and ask that you honor us with your presence at the temple to compose the text. An auspicious date has already been chosen, so there can be no delay.” Xiao Rang said, “I can only compose the inscription and write out the final calligraphy; I have no other useful skill. If you intend to erect a stele, you will also need a craftsman to carve the characters.” Dai Zong replied, “I have another fifty taels of silver with which to engage Jin Dajian, the Jade-Armed Craftsman, to carve the stone. Since the auspicious day is fixed, I earnestly beg you to show me where to find him, so that you may travel together.”

Taking one or two hundred taels of silver, he strapped the magic journey-talisman horses to his legs, descended the mountain, crossed by boat to Golden Sands Beach, went ashore, and sped toward Jizhou.

In less than four hours he was already inside the city. When he asked where Xiao Rang, the Sacred-Handed Scholar, lived, someone told him, “His home is just east of the prefectural offices, in front of the Confucian temple.”
Dai Zong went straight to the door, cleared his throat, and called, “Is Master Xiao at home?”
A scholar came out from within.
He did not recognize Dai Zong and asked, “Where have you come from, good attendant?
What business brings you here?”

ja: はくぎんごじゅうりょう
u.src: After bowing, Dai Zong said, “I am a temple attendant who prepares offerings at the Temple of the Sacred Peak in Taianzhou. We are now rebuilding the Tower of the Five Sacred Peaks, and the wealthy families of our prefecture wish to have an inscription carved on a stele. They have therefore sent me especially with fifty taels of silver for your household expenses and ask that you honor us with your presence at the temple to compose the text.
An auspicious date has already been chosen, so there can be no delay.”
Xiao Rang said, “I can only compose the inscription and write out the final calligraphy; I have no other useful skill.
If you intend to erect a stele, you will also need a craftsman to carve the characters.”
Dai Zong replied, “I have another fifty taels of silver with which to engage Jin Dajian, the Jade-Armed Craftsman, to carve the stone.
Since the auspicious day is fixed, I earnestly beg you to show me where to find him, so that you may travel together.”

p.src: Having received the fifty taels, Xiao Rang went with Dai Zong to seek out Jin Dajian. Just as they passed the Confucian temple, Xiao Rang pointed and said, “The man coming toward us is Jin Dajian, the Jade-Armed Craftsman.” Xiao Rang called Jin Dajian to a halt and introduced him to Dai Zong. He explained in full that the Tower of the Five Sacred Peaks at the Temple of the Sacred Peak in Taianzhou was being rebuilt, and that the wealthy families wished to erect an inscribed stone stele. “This attendant has come especially with fifty taels apiece to invite you and me there.” Jin Dajian was delighted when he saw the silver. The two invited Dai Zong into a wine shop, bought three cups of wine and some vegetable dishes, and entertained him. Dai Zong handed Jin Dajian fifty taels of silver for his household expenses, then said, “The diviner has already chosen the date. May I trouble you both to set out today?” Xiao Rang said, “The weather is warm. Even if we set out today, we will not travel far and will not reach the next lodging place ahead. It would be better to rise at the fifth watch tomorrow and leave as soon as the gates open.” Jin Dajian said, “That is exactly right.” The two agreed to depart early the next morning, then returned separately to their homes to pack what they needed. Xiao Rang kept Dai Zong at his home for the night.

p.src: At the fifth watch the next day, Jin Dajian came carrying his bundle and equipment, and set out together with Xiao Rang and Dai Zong. After they had left Jizhou and traveled little more than ten li, Dai Zong said, “Please take your time, gentlemen; I would not presume to hurry you. I shall go ahead and tell the wealthy patrons to come and welcome you.” Lengthening his stride, he hurried away ahead of them. The other two, with their bundles on their backs, continued slowly on their way. By the time they had nearly reached the hour of the Goat, they had covered some seventy or eighty li. Suddenly a piercing whistle sounded ahead, and from below a hill by the mountain stronghold sprang a band of some forty or fifty men. The hero at their head was none other than Wang Ying the Stumpy Tiger of Clear Breeze Mountain. He roared, “Who are you two? Where are you going? Lads, seize these fellows and cut out their hearts to go with our wine!” Xiao Rang pleaded, “We two are going to Taianzhou to carve an inscription in stone. We have not a penny of wealth between us, only a few articles of clothing.” Wang Ying shouted, “We do not want your money or clothing. We want the hearts and livers of two clever men to accompany our wine!” Driven to desperation, Xiao Rang and Jin Dajian trusted in their own abilities, leveled their staves, and charged straight at Wang Ying. Wang Ying raised his broad-bladed saber and fought them both. The three wielded their weapons and fought for five or seven bouts, whereupon Wang Ying turned and fled. The two were about to pursue him when another gong sounded on the mountain. From the left came Song Wan, the Giant in the Clouds; from the right came Du Qian, the Sky-Touching One; and behind them was Zheng Tianshou, the Fair-Faced Gentleman. Each led more than thirty men. They rushed forward together, knocked Xiao Rang and Jin Dajian down, dragged them away, and carried them into the woods. The four heroes said, “Set your minds at ease. We have come on the orders of Heavenly King Chao expressly to invite you both up the mountain to join our band.” Xiao Rang said, “What use could the stronghold have for us? Neither of us has the strength to truss a chicken; we are only good at eating.” Du Qian said, “First, Strategist Wu is acquainted with you; second, he knows the arts and skills you both possess. That is why he specially sent Dai Zong to your homes to invite you.” Xiao Rang and Jin Dajian stared at each other, unable to utter a word. They all went at once to the tavern of Zhu Gui, the Dry-Land Crocodile, where the customary wine and food were served. That very night they summoned a boat and conveyed the two men up the mountain. When they reached the great stronghold, Chao Gai, Wu Yong, and all the other chieftains met them. A banquet was at once prepared, and the matter of forging Cai Jing’s reply was explained. “That is why we have invited you two to join us on the mountain and unite in our great cause.” When the two heard this, they seized Scholar Wu by the arms and said, “We do not mind serving you here, but regrettably both our families, old and young, remain behind. If the authorities learn of this tomorrow, they will surely come to harm.” Wu Yong said, “My worthy brothers, do not worry. By daybreak all will be made clear.” That night they did nothing but drink, and then retired to rest.

p.src: At daybreak the next morning, a young bandit came to report, “They have all arrived.” Scholar Wu said, “My worthy brothers, please go in person to welcome your honored families.” Hearing this, Xiao Rang and Jin Dajian could only half believe it. When the two descended halfway down the mountain, they saw several sedan chairs carrying the old and young of both households up the slope. The two were struck dumb with astonishment and asked for the full story. Their families said, “After you left home yesterday, these men arrived with sedan chairs. They said that the master of the house had suffered heatstroke at an inn outside the city and that his family must be brought quickly to tend him. Once we were out of the city, they would not allow us to leave the chairs and carried us straight here.” Both families told the same story. When Xiao Rang heard this, he and Jin Dajian were left speechless. They had no choice but to resign themselves completely and return to the mountain stronghold to join the band. They settled the old and young of both households into lodgings. Scholar Wu then summoned Xiao Rang and consulted with him about writing a reply in Cai Jing’s hand to save Song Gongming. Jin Dajian said, “I have long carved seals of every kind bearing Cai Jing’s names, personal name, and style.” The two immediately set to work and completed the task. Once the reply had been prepared, a banquet was laid, and Dai Zong was sent on his way with detailed instructions concerning the letter’s contents. Dai Zong took leave of the assembled chieftains and descended the mountain. The young bandits had already ferried a boat across Golden Sands Beach, and they escorted him to Zhu Gui’s tavern. Dai Zong took four magic journey-talisman horses and strapped them to his legs. After bidding Zhu Gui farewell, he lengthened his stride and set out on the road.

p.src: Now Wu Yong, having seen Dai Zong across the ferry, returned with the other chieftains to the feast in the stronghold. While they were drinking, Scholar Wu suddenly cried out in dismay, with no regard for what the others might think. The chieftains asked, “Why do you cry out in dismay, Strategist?” Wu Yong replied, “None of you understand. That letter of mine has instead doomed Dai Zong and Song Gongming to death!” The chieftains were greatly alarmed and hurriedly asked, “What mistake was there in your letter, Strategist?” Scholar Wu said, “In my haste I considered only what came before and not what would follow. There is a grave inconsistency in the letter.” Xiao Rang said, “The handwriting I produced is exactly like Grand Preceptor Cai’s, and there is no error in the wording either. May I ask, Strategist, where this inconsistency lies?” Jin Dajian added, “I dare say the seal I carved is not wrong by so much as a hair. How can you tell that there is an inconsistency?” Scholar Wu brought two fingers together and explained where the mistake and inconsistency lay. And thus it came about that the heroes would throw Jiangzhou into turmoil and set the White Dragon Temple seething like a cauldron. They would flee for their lives through volleys of bows and crossbows, and rescue the heroes amid a forest of blades and spears. As for the precise inconsistency Strategist Wu revealed, listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
